It was believed that the cutoff for round objects is somewhere between 100 km and 200 km in radius if they have a large amount of ice in their makeup;[[1]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-1) however, later studies revealed that icy satellites as large as [Iapetus](Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (1,470 kilometers in diameter) are not in hydrostatic equilibrium at this time,[[2]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-2) and a 2019 assessment suggests that many TNOs in the size range of 400–1,000 kilometers may not even be fully solid bodies, much less gravitationally rounded.[[3]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-3) Objects that are ellipsoids due to their own gravity are here generally referred to as being "round", whether or not they are actually in equilibrium today, while objects that are clearly not ellipsoidal are referred to as being "irregular."

Spheroidal bodies typically have some polar flattening due to the [centrifugal force](Centrifugal_force "Centrifugal force") from their rotation, and can sometimes even have quite different equatorial diameters (scalene [ellipsoids](Ellipsoid "Ellipsoid") such as <Haumea>). Unlike bodies such as Haumea, the irregular bodies have a significantly non-ellipsoidal profile, often with sharp edges.

There can be difficulty in determining the diameter (within a factor of about 2) for typical objects beyond Saturn. (See [2060 Chiron](2060_Chiron#Physical_characteristics "2060 Chiron") as an example) For TNOs there is some confidence in the diameters, but for non-binary TNOs there is no real confidence in the masses/densities. Many TNOs are often just assumed to have Pluto's density of 2.0 g/cm3, but it is just as likely that they have a comet-like density of only 0.5 g/cm3.[[4]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-Britt2006-4)

For example, if a TNO is incorrectly assumed to have a mass of 3.59×1020 kg based on a radius of 350 km with a density of 2 g/cm3 but is later discovered to have a radius of only 175 km with a density of 0.5 g/cm3, its true mass would be only 1.12×1019 kg.

The sizes and masses of many of the moons of Jupiter and Saturn are fairly well known due to numerous observations and interactions of the *[Galileo](Galileo_(spacecraft) "Galileo (spacecraft)")* and *[Cassini](Cassini%E2%80%93Huygens "Cassini–Huygens")* orbiters; however, many of the moons with a radius less than ~100 km, such as Jupiter's [Himalia](Himalia_(moon) "Himalia (moon)"), have far less certain masses.[[5]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-jplssd-5) Further out from Saturn, the sizes and masses of objects are less clear. There has not yet been an orbiter around Uranus or Neptune for long-term study of their moons. For the small outer [irregular moons](Irregular_moon "Irregular moon") of Uranus, such as [Sycorax](Sycorax_(moon) "Sycorax (moon)"), which were not discovered by the *[Voyager 2](Voyager_2 "Voyager 2")* flyby, even different NASA web pages, such as the [National Space Science Data Center](National_Space_Science_Data_Center "National Space Science Data Center")[[6]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-nssdc-6) and JPL Solar System Dynamics,[[5]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-jplssd-5) give somewhat contradictory size and [albedo](Astronomical_albedo "Astronomical albedo") estimates depending on which research paper is being cited.

There are uncertainties in the figures for mass and radius, and irregularities in the shape and density, with accuracy often depending on how close the object is to Earth or whether it has been visited by a probe.

- Relative masses of the solid bodies of the Solar System. <Earth> at 48% and <Venus> at 39% dominate. Bodies less massive than <Pluto> are not visible at this scale.

- Relative masses of the rounded moons of the Solar System. [Mimas](Mimas_(moon) "Mimas (moon)"), <Enceladus>, and [Miranda](Miranda_(moon) "Miranda (moon)") are too small to be visible at this scale.

## Objects with radius over 400 km

The following objects have a mean radius of at least 400 km. It was once expected that any icy body larger than approximately 200 km in radius was likely to be in [hydrostatic equilibrium](Hydrostatic_equilibrium "Hydrostatic equilibrium") (HE).[[7]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-Brown-dplist-7) However, [Ceres](Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (r = 470 km) is the smallest body for which detailed measurements are consistent with hydrostatic equilibrium,[[8]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-8) whereas [Iapetus](Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (r = 735 km) is the largest icy body that has been found to not be in hydrostatic equilibrium.[[9]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-9) The known icy moons in this range are all ellipsoidal (except [Proteus](Proteus_(moon) "Proteus (moon)")), but trans-Neptunian objects up to 450–500 km radius may be quite porous.[[10]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-Grundy2019-10)

For simplicity and comparative purposes, the values are manually calculated assuming that the bodies are all spheres. The size of solid bodies does not include an object's atmosphere. For example, Titan looks bigger than Ganymede, but its solid body is smaller. For the [giant planets](Giant_planet "Giant planet"), the "radius" is defined as the distance from the center at which the atmosphere reaches 1 bar of atmospheric pressure.[[11]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-11)

Because Sedna and 2002 MS4 have no known moons, directly determining their mass is impossible without sending a probe (estimated to be from 1.7x1021 to 6.1×1021 kg for Sedna[[12]](List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size#cite_note-12)).

content:
Based on the Wikipedia article "List of Solar System objects by size," here are the mean radii of the eight planets in our Solar System:

| Planet | Mean Radius (km) |
|--------|------------------|
| **Jupiter** | 69,911 ± 6 km |
| **Saturn** | 58,232 ± 6 km |
| **Uranus** | 25,362 ± 7 km |
| **Neptune** | 24,622 ± 19 km |
| **Earth** | 6,371.0084 ± 0.0001 km |
| **Venus** | 6,052 ± 1 km |
| **Mars** | 3,389.5 ± 0.2 km |
| **Mercury** | 2,439.4 ± 0.1 km |

**Key observations:**
- **Jupiter** is by far the largest planet, with a radius nearly 11 times that of Earth
- The **gas giants** (Jupiter and Saturn) have the largest radii
- The **ice giants** (Uranus and Neptune) have similar radii, both around 4 times Earth's radius
- The **terrestrial planets** (Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury) are much smaller, with Earth and Venus being similar in size, while Mars has about half Earth's radius and Mercury has even less
- For the giant planets, the "radius" is defined as the distance from the center at which the atmosphere reaches 1 bar of atmospheric pressure

These values are from NASA's Solar System Dynamics database and represent the mean (average) radius of each planet in kilometers.
